hints: Focus on the key clue that azide behaves like chloride, so think first about what $\text{Cl}^-$ does with acidified silver nitrate.
Use charges to work out the formula, $\text{Ag}^+$ is +1 and $\text{N}_3^-$ is -1, just like $\text{Ag}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$.
Remember what happens to fresh white $\text{AgCl}$ in dilute aqueous ammonia, then apply that same behaviour to the azide precipitate.
walkthrough:
**Recall the test for chloride ions**

Think like a teacher. What do you already know? Acidified $\text{AgNO}_3$ gives a white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$ with $\text{Cl}^-$.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s) \text{ white precipitate}$$

Since $\text{N}_3^-$ is said to be similar to $\text{Cl}^-$, we expect a similar white silver salt.

**Deduce the correct formula**

Silver is $\text{Ag}^+$ and azide is $\text{N}_3^-$. Both ions have a single charge, so they combine 1:1 for neutrality.

$$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{N}_3^- \rightarrow \text{AgN}_3$$

This rules out $\text{Ag}_3\text{N}$. That would be silver nitride, where nitride is $\text{N}^{3-}$, not the azide ion $\text{N}_3^-$.

**Predict the effect of aqueous ammonia**

Fresh $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia to form a colourless complex solution.

$$\text{AgCl}(s) + 2\text{NH}_3(aq) \rightarrow [\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$$

By analogy, $\text{AgN}_3$ should also dissolve to give a colourless solution containing $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$. That matches a white precipitate of $\text{AgN}_3$ that dissolves.

options.A: Correct. The 1:1 combination of $\text{Ag}^+$ and $\text{N}_3^-$ gives $\text{AgN}_3$, analogous to $\text{AgCl}$. Like $\text{AgCl}$, it is white and dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia to form the colourless diamminesilver(I) complex, $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+.$
options.B: Formula $\text{AgN}_3$ is right, but the observation is wrong. Saying the precipitate remains confuses $\text{AgCl}$ behaviour with $\text{AgBr}$ (partly soluble) or $\text{AgI}$ (insoluble). White $\text{AgCl}$-like salts dissolve in dilute $\text{NH}_3$.
options.C: Observation of dissolving is right, but formula $\text{Ag}_3\text{N}$ is wrong. This is the classic trap of confusing azide, $\text{N}_3^-$, with nitride, $\text{N}^{3-}$. Azide has an overall 1- charge, so only one $\text{Ag}^+$ is needed.
options.D: Both parts are wrong. $\text{Ag}_3\text{N}$ incorrectly treats the ion as $\text{N}^{3-}$ instead of $\text{N}_3^-$, and a chloride-like white precipitate should dissolve in aqueous ammonia, not remain.
